skills.title: First Nations and Métis Communities Long Ago
skills.description: Between 1780 and 1850, First Nations and Métis communities lived in many places, and some had to move. Match each community to where it lived on a map.

skills.title: Settler Communities Long Ago
skills.description: Settlers like the French, Scots, Loyalists, and Black settlers made new communities. Match each group to the place where it settled on a map.

skills.title: Why Settlements Grew Where They Did
skills.description: Rivers, good soil, the fur trade, mills, and roads helped towns grow. Pick what made a place a good spot to live.

skills.title: Challenges Communities Faced
skills.description: Long ago, people faced hard weather, isolation, sickness, and unfair treatment. Match each challenge to a community that faced it.

skills.title: How Settlements Changed the Land
skills.description: Trading posts, farms, and towns changed nature and the people nearby. Pick what each kind of settlement did.

skills.title: Daily Life and Roles Long Ago
skills.description: Food, clothing, homes, and jobs for men, women, and children were different in each community. Match each to the right group.

skills.title: Treaties and Wampum Belts
skills.description: Treaties and wampum belts, like the Two Row Wampum, were agreements between peoples. Match each one to what it did.

skills.title: Conflict or Cooperation?
skills.description: Communities shared medicines and farms, but also fought over land. Sort each story into conflict or cooperation.

skills.title: Everyday Life Then: Same and Different
skills.description: Compare homes, clothes, food, work, and play of different groups from 1780 to 1850. Sort what was the same and what was different.

skills.title: Indigenous Life and Colonial Policies
skills.description: First Nations, Métis, and Inuit communities lived on and learned from the land. Later, residential schools and lost land changed their lives. Match each to before or after.

skills.title: Roles and Challenges Then and Now
skills.description: Jobs for women, men, and children and the problems people faced have changed since 1850. Sort what is from long ago and what is from today.

skills.title: What Makes Canada, Canada
skills.description: Two official languages, treaties, the kayak, lacrosse, and maple syrup are part of Canada's identity. Match each to the community it came from.

skills.title: Questions About Long Ago Challenges
skills.description: Pick a good question you could investigate about a challenge people faced from 1780 to 1850 and what they did about it.

skills.title: Sources About the Past
skills.description: Journals, artefacts, old paintings, and oral histories are sources. Sort which ones help answer a question about long ago.

skills.title: Maps of Long Ago
skills.description: Read maps of settlements, routes, and territories from 1780 to 1850. Pick what a thematic map shows.

skills.title: Timelines and Matrixes About the Past
skills.description: Use timelines, maps, and a chart to see how challenges and settlement changed things. Pick what the tool shows.

skills.title: Conclusions About Past Challenges
skills.description: Look at the evidence about a challenge and how people solved it. Pick the conclusion the evidence supports.

skills.title: Sharing History Findings
skills.description: Pick the best way to share what you learned, and the right words like treaty, settler, Loyalist, and hardship.

skills.title: Ontario Regions and Local Governments
skills.description: Ontario has cities, towns, counties, First Nations, and Métis regions. Match each to who leads it and the services it gives.

skills.title: Map Lettering Styles
skills.description: On political maps, countries, provinces, and cities are written in different styles. Pick which style fits each one.

skills.title: Ontario Landform Regions
skills.description: Ontario has the Canadian Shield, the Great Lakes–St. Lawrence Lowlands, and the Hudson Bay Lowlands. Match each region to what it is like.

skills.title: Types of Land Use
skills.description: Land is used for farms, factories, shops, homes, play, roads, and protecting nature. Match each use to the need it meets.

skills.title: Jobs in Ontario Regions
skills.description: People work in jobs like mining, tourism, schools, arts, and caring for land. Match jobs to the kind of region where they are found.

skills.title: Nature and Land Use Connections
skills.description: Ports grow on lakes, farms on flat rich soil, and resource towns near ore or trees. Match each natural feature to what gets built there.

skills.title: Nature and Jobs Connections
skills.description: Lakes bring tourism jobs, forests bring paper jobs, and Niagara Falls brings visitors. Match each place to the jobs its nature creates.

skills.title: Population and Land Use Patterns
skills.description: Read city and land-use maps to see where people live and how land is used. Pick the pattern the map shows.

skills.title: Comparing Land Use in Two Places
skills.description: Compare roads, parks, farmland, and shops in two places. Sort what is the same and what is different.

skills.title: Making Ontario Maps
skills.description: Pick the title, legend, direction arrow, and scale in kilometres to make a map of land uses or landform regions.

skills.title: Questions About Land Use Effects
skills.description: Pick a good question to investigate about how mining, farming, or building affects nature and what people do to help.

skills.title: Gathering Land Use Information
skills.description: Photos, interviews with Elders, park websites, and recycling facts are sources. Sort which ones tell about land use effects.

skills.title: Maps of Land Use Effects
skills.description: Use maps and atlases to find boundaries, land uses, and resources in a region. Pick what a map shows about the land.

skills.title: Graphs and Organizers About Land Use
skills.description: Read a line graph, bar graph, or organizer about forest cover or a mine. Pick the trend or effect it shows.

skills.title: Conclusions About Land Use and Nature
skills.description: Look at the evidence about short and long term effects of land use. Pick the conclusion it supports and the best way to reduce harm.

skills.title: Sharing Land Use Findings
skills.description: Pick the best way to share what you learned, and the right words like stewardship, pollution, population, and natural resources.
